subject: Banking
title: The 2008 Financial Crisis
description: A 1-minute de-risking session on The 2008 Financial Crisis.

hook.text: In September 2008, Lehman Brothers collapsed. The global financial system nearly stopped working within 48 hours.

buildup.text: Banks had packaged risky mortgages into securities and sold them worldwide.

discovery.text: Banks were so interconnected that one failure threatened them all.

twist.text: Governments spent $2 trillion bailing out banks. The people who caused the crisis kept their bonuses.

climax.text: 2008 proved that modern banking risk is global. A mortgage default in Ohio can bankrupt a bank in Germany.

punchline.text: One bank fell. The whole world felt it. 2008 changed banking forever.

details.summary: The 2008 financial crisis began with US subprime mortgage defaults, cascaded through complex bank securities, and froze global credit markets. The resulting Great Recession was the worst economic downturn since the 1930s Depression.
details.whyItMatters: The 2008 crisis reshaped banking regulation, destroyed trillions in wealth, and affected billions of lives. It remains the defining financial event of the 21st century and the reference point for all current banking policy.
takeaways: Subprime mortgage defaults triggered cascading failures across the financial system
Global bank bailouts and stimulus exceeded $10 trillion
The crisis led to Dodd-Frank regulation and the Basel III capital framework

faq.question: How did the 2008 crisis spread from mortgages to the entire economy?
faq.answer: Banks had packaged subprime mortgages into securities sold worldwide. When mortgages defaulted, these securities lost value, destroying bank capital globally. Banks stopped lending to each other, freezing credit and causing businesses to fail across all sectors.

faq.question: What did the 2008 crisis change about banking?
faq.answer: Banks now hold significantly more capital, face regular stress tests, and operate under stricter rules. The Dodd-Frank Act created new oversight agencies, restricted risky trading, and established mechanisms for orderly bank resolution.
